title: The Secret Lines of Torres Vedras
text:
In October 1809 Lord Wellington (he became a duke only in 1814), commanding the British and Portuguese forces in Portugal, expected a much larger French army to invade again. He gave secret orders to his chief engineer, Richard Fletcher, to fortify the hills north of Lisbon. Over the next year thousands of Portuguese laborers built lines of forts, redoubts, ditches and dammed rivers across the peninsula between the Atlantic and the Tagus. Few people outside the project, including in London, understood their scale.

In 1810 Marshal Andre Massena invaded Portugal. Wellington fought a delaying action at Bussaco and then withdrew south. At the same time the Portuguese authorities ordered the countryside in front of the French cleared: crops gathered or destroyed, mills disabled, people moved behind the lines.

In October 1810 Massena arrived before Torres Vedras and found a barrier he had not known existed. He probed it, judged it too strong to attack, and after a month in front of it fell back to Santarem, hoping the British would weaken first. Instead his own army starved in the stripped land, while Wellington's troops were supplied by sea. In March 1811 Massena retreated to Spain, having lost many thousands of men to hunger and disease without fighting a major battle at the lines.
lesson: Quiet preparation done long before it is needed can decide a contest. Pick a position the opponent cannot afford to attack and let time and logistics work for you.
people: Arthur Wellesley, Viscount Wellington, Richard Fletcher, Andre Massena
source: The Dispatches of Field Marshal the Duke of Wellington; Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, vols. 3 and 4
